bib.title: APIGen: Automated Pipeline for Generating Verifiable and Diverse Function-Calling Datasets

legacy_report:
SOURCE: APIGen: Automated PIpeline for Generating Verifiable and Diverse Function-Calling Datasets. Zuxin Liu, Thai Hoang, Jianguo Zhang, ... Caiming Xiong (Salesforce AI Research). arXiv:2406.18518v1, preprint ("Preprint." printed), 2024-06-26.

COVERAGE: All 20 of 20 pages read (62,092 chars extracted). Body, Table 1, Table 2, appendices A.2-B.3 read. The references block (roughly chars 42,500-47,000) was only skimmed in part. Figures 1-5 are images and were not viewed. Text extraction was clean, apart from spaced-out JSON in the appendix.

CLAIMS
- Claim: APIGen is a three-stage verification pipeline (format, execution, semantic) for synthetic function-calling data. Its key insight is that function-call answers can be executed, unlike free chat data.
  number: none (3 stages)
  setup: single-turn calls only. Backends are Python functions (run in a subprocess) and REST APIs. The semantic stage is an LLM judge.
  quote: "function-calling answers can be directly executed via their corresponding APIs. This enables checking if the output API and parameters' formats are correct, if the generated API calls are executable, and if execution results match the query's intent"
  where: Sec 3.2, p4
- Claim: xLAM-7B(FC), trained on APIGen data, ranked 6th on BFCL, ahead of GPT-4o (FC) and GPT-4-turbo (FC).
  number: 85.65 overall, vs 82.94 for GPT-4o-2024-05-13 (FC) and 82.88 for GPT-4-turbo-2024-04-09 (FC). Rank 1 was GPT-4-0125-Preview (Prompt) at 88.
  setup: DeepSeek-Coder-7B-instruct-v1.5 fine-tuned with the xLAM/AgentOhana pipeline. BFCL snapshot as of 06/15/2024, about 2,000 test cases. The leaderboard has since moved.
  quote: "6 85.65 xLAM-7B (FC) 80.55 96 90 87.5 90.59 90 86 77.5 80.42"
  where: Table 2, p8
- Claim: xLAM-1B(FC) ranked 24th and beat GPT-3.5-Turbo-0125 and Claude-3 Haiku.
  number: 74.41 vs 63.88 (GPT-3.5-Turbo-0125 FC) and 74.29 (Claude-3-Haiku, Prompt mode)
  setup: DeepSeek-Coder-1.3B-instruct, same pipeline and snapshot. The Haiku margin is only 0.12. The text lists Haiku among models xLAM-1B "outperforms", but Haiku was tested in prompt mode.
  quote: "24 74.41 xLAM-1B (FC) 75.09 80.5 76.5 63 79.41 80 78 62.5 72.08"
  where: Table 2, p8
- Claim: Generator strength drives the pass rate. The weaker open models produced mostly unexecutable calls. The authors say weaker generators need strict verification.
  number: pass rate 34.42% (DeepSeek-Coder-33B), 38.46% (Mixtral-8x7B), 65.96% (Mixtral-8x22B), 84.15% (DeepSeek-V2-Chat 236B)
  setup: target 40,000 generations per model, temperature 0.7, sampled APIs, seeds and prompts. In every model except DeepSeek-V2-Chat, execution failures are the largest rejection bucket.
  quote: "DeepSeek-Coder-33B-Inst 13,769 4,311 15,496 6,424 34.42%"
  where: Table 1, p7
- Claim: Format and execution checks reject most bad data. These failures include hallucinated functions or parameters, wrong types and missing required parameters.
  number: none beyond Table 1
  setup: the same runs as Table 1.
  quote: "The first two stages, format checker and execution checker, typically filter out the majority of low-quality data."
  where: Sec 4.2, p6-7
- Claim: Ablation. Adding back the data rejected at the execution and semantic stages lowers BFCL performance, and the drop is larger for the smaller model.
  number: none in text (shown in Fig 5 only; the values were not extracted)
  setup: xLAM-1B and xLAM-7B, BFCL.
  quote: "using these filtered datasets for training harms the final performance, with a more significant impact on the smaller model"
  where: Sec 5.2, p9
- Claim: Human check of the released data found about 95% good.
  number: 28 of 600 had minor issues (about 95.3% good, as the paper says)
  setup: 3 human evaluators on 600 samples from the released set. The criteria were parameter accuracy and the number of calls.
  quote: "only 28 out of the 600 inspected samples have minor issues"
  where: App A.3, p15-16. Note the paper says "approximately 95.3%", but 572/600 is 95.33%.
- Claim: The released dataset is 60k entries over 3,673 executable APIs in 21 categories, with parallel and parallel-multiple query styles that the authors call rare in public data.
  number: 60,000 entries; 3,539 REST APIs (cleaned from ToolBench's 16,464) plus 134 Python functions = 3,673
  setup: the entries come from Mixtral-8x22B and DeepSeek-V2-Chat only. The four query styles are simple, multiple, parallel and parallel multiple.
  quote: "After cleaning, we obtain 3,539 executable REST APIs with good documentation." and "We collected 134 well-documented Python functions"
  where: Sec 4.1, p6
- Claim: Relevance-detection data was added for training. In these examples the tool is irrelevant or a required argument is missing, and the correct output is an empty tool call.
  number: 8,000 data points
  setup: built by randomly dropping the tools that the answer calls, or dropping required parameters. Appendix B.3.
  quote: "We create 8,000 such data points from the collected dataset by 1) randomly discarding some tools that will be called in the answer or 2) randomly dropping some required parameters"
  where: App B.3, p19
- Claim: Training setup.
  number: lr 5e-6, 4 epochs, AdamW, 8x A100 40GB, cutoff 2048
  setup: details in B.3
  quote: "a learning rate of 5 × 10−6, four epochs, and use of the AdamW optimizer"
  where: App B.3, p20

LIMITS
- The authors concede the framework covers only REST APIs and Python functions, and only single-turn function calling. They list multi-turn interaction as future work.
- Evaluation is on BFCL alone, as of 06/15/2024. The ranking is dated, and the paper has no ablation of the three checkers beyond execution and semantic.
- The semantic checker is an LLM and its error rate is not measured separately. Only the 600-sample human check bounds quality.
- The ablation values are in Fig 5 and were not extracted.
- Comparisons mix FC and Prompt modes.
- The paper does not compare against ReAct loops or multi-step tool use.

BUILDS ON: Berkeley Function-Calling Leaderboard (Yan et al. 2024) for query styles and the eval; ToolBench/ToolLLM (Qin et al. 2023) for the 16,464 RapidAPI APIs and the StableToolBench server; AgentOhana/xLAM (Zhang et al. 2024) for the training pipeline; chain-of-thought (Wei et al.) for the "thought" field; LIMA-style quality-over-quantity argument (ref [36]); Toolformer, Gorilla, NexusRaven and Gorilla OpenFunctions-v2 as related work.

CODE: Training prompt output format (App B.3, p19-20): `{"tool_calls": [{"name": "func_name1", "arguments": {"argument1": "value1"}}]}`, with an empty list when no tool fits or a parameter is missing. Semantic checker output (App B.2, p18): `{"thought": "...", "pass": "yes" or "no"}`. Dataset record shape (A.2): query, tools[{name, description, parameters{type, description, required}}], answers[{name, arguments}].

FIGURES: Fig 1 (p2) function-calling agent workflow. Fig 2 (p3) the pipeline: samplers -> generator -> format -> execution -> semantic checkers, with passing data fed back into the seed set. Fig 5 (p9) the ablation of adding back the filtered data. Figures were not viewed.

NOTE FOR TARGET NOTE (02-tool-use-and-react.md): the note's Gorilla/ToolLLM paragraph (the "field tried two fixes in 2023" passage) is the natural place for an APIGen row. The paper adds a third lever, training data verified by execution. It also matches the note's rule "Validate arguments before the tool runs" and "Return descriptive errors", because the Stage 2 executor returns fine-grained error types. The paper's relevance-detection training (refusing when the tool is missing or an argument is absent) is not in the note.

PROBLEMS: No embedded instructions found in the PDF. Fig 5 values and the Fig 4 category counts were not captured as text. The Table 2 rows 34-42 are elided ("...") in the source.
